planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring as soil becomes workable; this is the widely cultivated lady fern of the nursery trade, distinct from the North American native lady ferns Athyrium angustum and Athyrium asplenioides already carried in this dataset.

directions: Plant divisions or nursery starts in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, working compost into the planting hole and setting the crown level with the soil surface. Common lady fern forms a graceful clump of lance-shaped, finely twice-cut fronds that arch outward from a central crown, giving a light, airy texture to shaded borders and woodland plantings without the bulk of coarser ferns. It is the classic lady fern found across garden centers and breeding programs worldwide, having given rise to many of the crested, tatted, and dwarf lady fern cultivars sold today, while the straight species itself remains an easygoing, reliable choice for naturalizing under trees. Keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season, particularly in warmer climates where it dries and browns at the margins fastest, and cut the deciduous fronds back to the crown in late winter before the new fiddleheads unfurl.

planting.note: Plant crown divisions in early spring as soil becomes workable, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Astilbe japonica is one of the principal Japanese parent species behind the popular Astilbe x arendsii garden hybrids and blooms earlier than most of them.

directions: Plant crown divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, setting the crown just at or slightly below the soil surface and mulching well to conserve moisture. Astilbe japonica is a compact, early-flowering woodland species from Japan that sends up dense, upright plumes of white to soft pink flowers in late spring ahead of most of the Astilbe x arendsii hybrids bred from it, held above finely divided, glossy dark green foliage that stays tidy through summer. It spreads gradually into a well-behaved clump by short rhizomes and combines naturally with hostas, ferns, and other moisture-loving shade perennials in a woodland border. Keep the soil evenly moist all season, since this species scorches and browns at the leaf edges quickly once it dries out, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep them blooming vigorously.
